```text
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)      # outermost dimension (original C index i)
    q: dim in [0, NQ)      # middle dimension  (original C index j)
    p: dim in [0, NP)      # output component (original C index k)
    s: dim in [0, NP)      # reduction dimension over NP

data:
    # Input A(r, q, s) corresponds to original A[i][j][k] with k ≡ s.
    # Layout chosen so that s is the innermost/contiguous dimension for good streaming.
    A_in[r, q, s]: in  DATA_TYPE
        = (r, q, s) -> ((r * NQ + q) * NP + s)       # row-major, s contiguous

    # C4(s, p) corresponds to original C4[s][p].
    # Layout chosen so that p is contiguous: when we fix s and loop over p
    # (our innermost loop), we read a full row of C4 linearly.
    C4[s, p]:      in  DATA_TYPE
        = (s, p) -> (s * NP + p)                     # row-major, p contiguous

    # Output A_out(r, q, p) corresponds to updated A[i][j][p] after doitgen.
    # Layout chosen so that p is contiguous for vectorized stores.
    A_out[r, q, p]: out DATA_TYPE
        = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ + q) * NP + p)       # row-major, p contiguous

    # Local scratch buffer used per (r, q) to accumulate the NP outputs.
    # Size is NP; allocated per thread / per (r,q)-tile, so overall extra
    # memory is negligible vs A_in and A_out.
    tmp[p]: local DATA_TYPE                          # not part of global interface

parameters:
    # Tunable tile sizes (chosen empirically for the target machine).
    TILE_R: int      # tile size along r  (e.g., 4 or 8)
    TILE_Q: int      # tile size along q  (e.g., 4 or 8)
    TILE_P: int      # tile size along p  (e.g., 32 or 64; multiple of vector width)
    TILE_S: int      # tile size along s  (e.g., 8 or 16)

    # Vector width and unroll factor tuned for the x64 machine.
    VEC_P:   int     # vectorization width along p (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4 for double)
    UNROLL_S: int    # small unroll factor along s inside a tile (e.g., 4)

computation:
    # Mathematical specification:
    #   For all r, q, p:
    #       A_out[r, q, p] = sum_{s=0..NP-1} A_in[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # We implement this using a per-(r,q) temporary vector tmp[p] to
    # maximize reuse of A_in[r,q,s] and stream rows of C4[s,*].

    for r, q:
        # 1. Initialize accumulator vector for this (r, q).
        for p:
            tmp[p] = 0

        # 2. Accumulate contributions from all s.
        for s:
            a_val = A_in[r, q, s]          # loaded once and reused across all p
            for p:
                tmp[p] = tmp[p] + a_val * C4[s, p]

        # 3. Store the accumulated result.
        for p:
            A_out[r, q, p] = tmp[p]

optimization:
    # --- Cache- and thread-friendly blocking over r and q ---------------------
    # Process A in tiles over (r, q) so each thread works on a rectangular patch.
    block(r, R, TILE_R)     # r = R * TILE_R + r_in
    block(q, Q, TILE_Q)     # q = Q * TILE_Q + q_in

    # Hoist the tile loops to the outermost level to form:
    #   for R:
    #     for Q:
    #       for r in tile:
    #         for q in tile:
    hoist(R)
    hoist(Q)

    # Parallelize across the outer r-tiles. Each (R, Q)-tile is independent
    # because each (r, q) slice of A_out depends only on the corresponding
    # (r, q) slice of A_in and all of C4.
    parallelize(R)

    # --- Blocking and vectorization over p (output dimension) ----------------
    # We want p as the innermost loop for good spatial locality and
    # to expose vectorization opportunities on x64.
    block(p, P, TILE_P)     # outer tile index P, inner p within tile

    # Vectorize the inner p loop. Since C4[s, p] and A_out[r, q, p] both
    # have contiguous p-dimension, this generates coalesced vector loads
    # and stores.
    vectorize(p, VEC_P)

    # --- Blocking and unrolling over s (reduction dimension) ------------------
    # Tile s to improve temporal locality on C4 and A_in for large NP.
    block(s, S, TILE_S)

    # Hoist the tile loop S above p so we iterate:
    #   for S:    # over contiguous bands of s
    #     for s:
    #       a_val = A_in[r, q, s]
    #       for p (vectorized):
    #         tmp[p] += a_val * C4[s, p]
    #
    # This preserves the per-p accumulation order in s (we still visit s
    # in increasing order), but interleaves updates across different p
    # values. It is functionally equivalent to the original reduction.
    hoist(S)

    # Within each s-tile, unroll the reduction to expose instruction-level
    # parallelism and reduce loop overhead. TILE_S should be chosen so that
    # UNROLL_S divides it or is at most TILE_S.
    unroll(s, UNROLL_S)

    # --- Notes on locality and arithmetic ------------------------------------
    # - A_in is streamed along s; for each (r,q) we read each A_in[r,q,s]
    #   exactly once, reuse it for all p in vector registers, and never
    #   touch it again.
    # - C4 is accessed row-wise: for fixed s, C4[s, p] is read with p as
    #   innermost, so the mapping (s, p) -> s*NP + p produces contiguous
    #   loads that vectorize naturally.
    # - Using tmp[p] as an accumulator vector avoids repeatedly reading
    #   and writing A_out during the reduction and keeps partial sums in
    #   fast L1/cache or registers.
    # - Extra memory for tmp[p] is NP elements per active (r, q) tile,
    #   which is far less than 50% of the memory footprint of A_in/A_out.
```

```text
domain:
    # Logical iteration space (matches original C code semantics)
    r: dim in [0, NR)        # outermost dimension
    q: dim in [0, NQ)
    p: dim in [0, NP)        # output index
    s: dim in [0, NP)        # reduction index

data:
    # 3D tensor A: logically A_in[r,q,p] == original A[r][q][p]
    # Underlying storage is row-major in (r,q,p) order:
    #   offset_A(r,q,p) = ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p
    A_in[r, q, p]: in num_t = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p

    # 2D tensor C4 is stored transposed w.r.t. the original C4[s][p] for
    # better memory locality along the reduction dimension:
    #
    #   original:  C4_orig[s, p]  (row-major: offset = s * NP + p)
    #   stored as: C4_tr[p, s]   (row-major: offset = p * NP + s)
    #
    # So C4_tr[p,s] == C4_orig[s,p]. This matches the Halide mapping
    # C4_param(p, s) used in the code.
    C4_tr[p, s]: in num_t = (p, s) -> p * NP + s

    # Output tensor A_out: same logical layout as A_in
    A_out[r, q, p]: out num_t = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p

parameters:
    # Tunable blocking / vectorization parameters; concrete values
    # should be chosen based on cache sizes and SIMD width of the target.
    TILE_R: int  # e.g., 1, 2, 4  (NR is often small)
    TILE_Q: int  # e.g., 4, 8, 16
    TILE_P: int  # e.g., 32 or 64
    TILE_S: int  # e.g., 32 or 64

    VEC_P:  int  # vector width along p  (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float, 4 for AVX2 double)
    UNROLL_S: int  # small unroll factor for reduction (e.g., 4)

computation:
    # Mathematical definition (matches the Halide pipeline):
    #
    # For each (r,q,p):
    #   A_out[r,q,p] = sum_{s=0..NP-1} A_in[r,q,s] * C4_tr[p,s]
    #
    # Note: C4_tr[p,s] is the transpose of the original C4[s,p].
    for r, q, p:
        A_out[r, q, p] = sum(s in [0, NP), A_in[r, q, s] * C4_tr[p, s])

optimization:
    #-----------------------------
    # 1. Data-layout optimization
    #-----------------------------
    # C4 is stored as C4_tr[p,s] (transpose of original C4[s,p]) so that
    # inner-loop iteration over s or p can use unit-stride accesses
    # depending on loop ordering. This is already reflected in `data`.
    #
    # No extra buffer beyond A_in, C4_tr, A_out is required.

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 2. Loop reordering for better data reuse
    #---------------------------------------------
    # The mathematical definition uses an abstract sum over s. A naïve
    # implementation would typically produce the loop nest:
    #
    #   for r in [0,NR):
    #     for q in [0,NQ):
    #       for p in [0,NP):
    #         acc = 0
    #         for s in [0,NP):
    #           acc += A_in[r,q,s] * C4_tr[p,s]
    #         A_out[r,q,p] = acc
    #
    # This re-reads A_in[r,q,s] for every p, wasting bandwidth.
    #
    # We instead reorder loops to:
    #
    #   for r in [0,NR):
    #     for q in [0,NQ):
    #       for p in [0,NP): A_out[r,q,p] = 0      # initialization
    #       for s in [0,NP):                       # reduction outer
    #         for p in [0,NP):                     # p inner
    #           A_out[r,q,p] += A_in[r,q,s] * C4_tr[p,s]
    #
    # which loads each A_in[r,q,s] once and reuses it across all p.
    # This corresponds to interchanging the (p,s) order around the
    # reduction; it is mathematically valid because the reduction is
    # associative and commutative (up to FP roundoff).
    interchange(p, s)

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 3. Blocking (tiling) for cache locality
    #---------------------------------------------
    # Tile over r and q to create chunks that fit in cache. Inside each
    # (R,Q) tile, we operate over the full p and s spaces, but also tile
    # those to improve locality of C4_tr and A_out.
    block(r, R, TILE_R)    # r = R * TILE_R + r_inner
    block(q, Q, TILE_Q)    # q = Q * TILE_Q + q_inner
    block(p, P, TILE_P)    # p = P * TILE_P + p_inner
    block(s, S, TILE_S)    # s = S * TILE_S + s_inner
    # After blocking and the interchange above, a typical optimized order is:
    #   for R, Q (outer tiles)
    #     for S  (tiles of s)
    #       for P  (tiles of p)
    #         for s_inner
    #           for p_inner
    #             A_out[...] += A_in[...] * C4_tr[...]

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 4. Parallelism
    #---------------------------------------------
    # Different (r,q) tiles are independent; parallelize over outer
    # tiles to exploit multi-core CPU. We parallelize R, and (optionally)
    # Q if NR is small, to create enough work per thread.
    parallelize(R)
    # Optionally, if NR is very small and NQ is large:
    # parallelize(Q)

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 5. Vectorization and unrolling
    #---------------------------------------------
    # Vectorize along p_inner, which corresponds to contiguous memory
    # in both A_out and C4_tr (row-major with p as the leading dimension
    # inside the tile).
    vectorize(P, VEC_P)

    # Unroll a small number of iterations of the reduction over s_inner
    # to reduce loop overhead and expose ILP. TILE_S should be a
    # multiple of UNROLL_S for best effect.
    unroll(S, UNROLL_S)

    #---------------------------------------------
    # 6. Hoisting invariant work
    #---------------------------------------------
    # For each fixed (r,q,s_inner) inside a tile, A_in[r,q,s] does
    # not depend on p; the compiler should hoist its load out of the
    # inner p loop automatically. We express this intent by hoisting S
    # above P to the outermost possible level within each (R,Q) tile.
    #
    # This further encourages:
    #   tmp = A_in[r,q,s]
    #   for p_inner: A_out[...] += tmp * C4_tr[p_inner,s]
    hoist(S)
```

domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)          # corresponds to original A[NR][NQ][NP] index i
    q: dim in [0, NQ)          # original index j
    p: dim in [0, NP)          # original index k (output component)
    s: dim in [0, NP)          # reduction index over NP

data:
    A_in[r, q, p]: in num_t =
        (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p
        # Row‑major layout for original A[r][q][p]:
        #   fastest varying: p, then q, then r.

    C4[s, p]: in num_t =
        (s, p) -> s * NP + p
        # Row‑major layout for original C4[s][p]:
        #   fastest varying: p, then s.
        # This matches the access pattern C4[s, p] with p innermost.

    A_out[r, q, p]: out num_t =
        (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ) + q) * NP + p
        # Same layout as A_in; contains the updated A[r][q][p].

computation:
    # For each fixed (r, q) we conceptually compute
    #   A_out[r, q, p] = sum_{s=0..NP-1} A_in[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    # for all p. We structure the loops to reuse A_in[r, q, s] across
    # all p, so each A_in element is loaded once per (r, q) instead of
    # NP times, while preserving the mathematical result.

    for r, q:
        # Initialize the output row for this (r, q).
        for p:
            A_out[r, q, p] = 0

        # Sequential reduction over s for each (r, q).
        for s in seq([0, NP)):
            a_val = A_in[r, q, s]
            # Update all p components with this basis contribution.
            for p:
                A_out[r, q, p] = A_out[r, q, p] + a_val * C4[s, p]

optimization:
    # Tunable blocking / vectorization constants (compile-time or configuration):
    #   TR   – tile size in r  (e.g., 4)
    #   TQ   – tile size in q  (e.g., 8)
    #   TP   – tile size in p  (e.g., 64, multiple of SIMD width)
    #   TS   – tile size in s  (e.g., 32)
    #   VEC_P – SIMD width for p (e.g., 8 for AVX2 fp64 / 16 for fp32)
    #   US   – unroll factor for inner s loop (e.g., 4)
    #
    # These do not change the mathematical result; they only affect
    # performance and can be tuned for a given machine.

    # 1. Tile the (r, q) iteration space to improve locality and expose
    #    coarse-grain parallelism.
    block(r, R_tile, TR)      # r = R_tile * TR + r_in
    block(q, Q_tile, TQ)      # q = Q_tile * TQ + q_in

    # 2. Tile the (p, s) space to build a small, cache-friendly kernel.
    #    This allows reusing tiles of C4 and A_in rows in L1/L2.
    block(p, P_tile, TP)      # p = P_tile * TP + p_in
    block(s, S_tile, TS)      # s = S_tile * TS + s_in

    # 3. Hoist tile loops outward so that execution order is logically:
    #       for R_tile, Q_tile in outer tiles
    #         for r_in, q_in in tile
    #           for S_tile (chunks of s)
    #             for s_in in S_tile
    #               for P_tile (chunks of p)
    #                 for p_in in P_tile
    #    This lets each worker thread operate on a block of (r, q) pairs
    #    while reusing C4 and A_in[r, q, s] from cache.
    hoist(R_tile)
    hoist(Q_tile)
    hoist(S_tile)
    hoist(P_tile)

    # 4. Parallelize across tiles of (r, q). All (r, q) pairs are
    #    independent, so separate threads can handle different tiles.
    parallelize(R_tile)
    parallelize(Q_tile)

    # 5. Ensure inner loops iterate with p_in innermost for contiguous,
    #    vectorizable accesses to A_out and C4.
    #    After tiling, we interchange so that for each (r_in, q_in, S_tile, s_in)
    #    we iterate over (P_tile, p_in) as the inner nest.
    interchange(S_tile, P_tile)
    interchange(s_in, p_in)

    # 6. Vectorize over p_in. For fixed (r, q, s) and a range of
    #    consecutive p_in, all operations are independent and touch
    #    contiguous elements of A_out and C4, which maps well to SIMD.
    vectorize(p_in, VEC_P)

    # 7. Unroll a small factor of s_in to increase ILP inside each TS tile,
    #    while keeping the overall reduction over s sequential.
    unroll(s_in, US)

    # 8. (Optional) If NP (and hence TP) is small, fully unroll p_in
    #    within a tile to eliminate loop overhead:
    #    # if TP is small:
    #    #     unroll(p_in, TP)

    # Summary of effects:
    #   - Each A_in[r, q, s] is loaded exactly once per (r, q) and reused
    #     across all p, greatly reducing memory traffic vs the naive
    #     per-(r, q, p) reduction.
    #   - C4 is accessed in contiguous p_in slices within each s_in, which
    #     is cache- and SIMD-friendly due to row-major layout C4[s, p].
    #   - Blocking (r, q) improves temporal locality of A_out rows and
    #     allows efficient multi-core parallelization across tiles.
    #   - Blocking (p, s), vectorizing p_in, and unrolling s_in build a
    #     tight inner kernel that exploits SIMD and ILP on a modern x64 CPU.

```text
domain:
    # Problem sizes from Polybench/defines.hpp
    r: dim in [0, NR)        # outermost dimension
    q: dim in [0, NQ)
    p: dim in [0, NP)
    s: dim in [0, NP)        # reduction dimension

data:
    # Original C layout:
    #   A[NR][NQ][NP] accessed as A[r][q][k]
    #   C4[NP][NP]     accessed as C4[s][p]
    #
    # We model two logical arrays, using a standard row-major layout
    # with the last index contiguous in memory.

    A_in[r, q, s]: in  DATA_TYPE
        = (r, q, s) -> ((r * NQ + q) * NP + s)
        # Row-major: for fixed (r, q), elements A_in[r, q, *] over s are
        # contiguous in memory. This matches the read pattern over s.

    C4[s, p]:     in  DATA_TYPE
        = (s, p) -> (s * NP + p)
        # Row-major: for fixed s, C4[s, *] over p are contiguous.
        # This matches the inner loop over p in the optimized computation.

    A_out[r, q, p]: out DATA_TYPE
        = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ + q) * NP + p)
        # Row-major: for fixed (r, q), outputs A_out[r, q, *] over p are
        # contiguous and will be updated in the innermost loop.

parameters:
    # No scalar coefficients in this kernel; everything comes from A_in and C4.
    # Tuning parameters for the schedule (chosen for a modern x64 CPU with
    # wide SIMD and sizable caches):
    TR: int  # tile size in r, e.g. 1–4
    TQ: int  # tile size in q, e.g. 4–16
    TP: int  # tile size in p, e.g. 64
    VP: int  # SIMD width for p, e.g. 8 or 16 depending on vector ISA
    US: int  # unroll factor for the reduction over s, e.g. 4 or 8

computation:
    # Semantics (matches the Halide and original C code):
    #   For each (r, q, p),
    #     A_out[r][q][p] = sum_{s=0..NP-1} A_in[r][q][s] * C4[s][p]
    #
    # We express this as an explicit two-pass update to make the loop
    # structure for optimization more apparent.

    init_A_out:
        for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ), p in [0, NP):
            A_out[r, q, p] = 0

    update_A_out:
        for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ):
            for s in [0, NP):
                let a = A_in[r, q, s]
                for p in [0, NP):
                    A_out[r, q, p] += a * C4[s, p]

dependencies:
    # Initialization must complete before any accumulation for each (r, q, p):
    for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ), p in [0, NP):
        init_A_out(r, q, p) -> update_A_out(r, q, *, p)

optimization:
    # High-level strategy:
    #   * Treat (r, q) as a 2D batch dimension: independent work, amenable to
    #     coarse-grain parallelism.
    #   * For a fixed (r, q), compute all p outputs together and reuse
    #     A_in[r, q, s] across all p by looping over s outside p.
    #   * Keep C4 in row-major layout so that C4[s, *] is contiguous and
    #     vectorize across p.
    #   * Tile r and q for cache locality and parallel work distribution.
    #   * Tile and vectorize p; partially unroll the reduction over s.

    # 1. Tile the outer spatial dimensions to create cache-friendly blocks
    #    and a parallel work grid over (r, q).
    #
    #    r = Rb * TR + r_i, where Rb is the r-tile index, r_i is intra-tile.
    #    q = Qb * TQ + q_i.
    block(r, Rb, TR)
    block(q, Qb, TQ)

    # 2. Parallelize over tiles in r (and optionally q if NR is small and NQ is large).
    #    This distributes independent (r, q)-blocks across the 32 physical cores.
    parallelize(Rb)
    # Optionally, if NQ is large relative to NR, we can also parallelize Qb.
    # parallelize(Qb)

    # 3. Within each (Rb, Qb) tile, we want the loop order:
    #       for r_i, q_i:
    #         for s:
    #           for p:
    #             ...
    #    so that:
    #      * A_in[r, q, s] is loaded once per (r, q, s) and reused across all p.
    #      * C4[s, p] has unit-stride access along p.
    #    The computation section is already written in this order, but we make
    #    the intent explicit:
    interchange(s, p)   # ensure that for each (r, q), s is outside p

    # 4. Tile and vectorize along the p dimension to exploit SIMD registers.
    #    p = Pb * TP + p_i, then within each tile, split p_i into vector lanes.
    block(p, Pb, TP)

    # Vectorize the innermost segment of p. VP should match the hardware
    # vector width in DATA_TYPE elements (e.g., 8 or 16 for float/double).
    vectorize(p, VP)

    # 5. Unroll the reduction over s moderately to increase ILP and reduce the
    #    loop overhead for the dot products. Since s is not the innermost
    #    vectorized dimension, unrolling does not harm vectorization.
    unroll(s, US)

    # 6. Optional blocking of the reduction dimension for very large NP.
    #    This can improve cache reuse of C4 when NP is large: each S-block
    #    of s works with a row stripe C4[s_block, *] that stays in caches.
    #
    #    # block(s, Sb, TS)
    #    # hoist(Sb)       # move the s-block loop just inside (r, q) tiles
    #
    #    We leave these commented as they are tuning knobs for very large NP.

    # Notes:
    #  - No extra temporaries are introduced; A_out is accumulated in-place
    #    (separate from A_in), so additional memory usage is negligible and
    #    well within the 50% overhead constraint.
    #  - This schedule maintains the original numerical result: changing the
    #    loop nesting over the associative + commutative reduction in s does
    #    not alter the mathematical semantics.
```

```text
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)          # outermost loop: original A[NR][NQ][NP] index 0
    q: dim in [0, NQ)          # middle loop:  original A[NR][NQ][NP] index 1
    p: dim in [0, NP)          # output coord: original A[NR][NQ][NP] index 2
    s: dim in [0, NP)          # reduction coord over NP

data:
    # Input 3D array A_in: original A[r][q][s], row‑major with p/s as fastest-varying index.
    # Layout: A_in[r, q, s] stored such that s is unit-stride in memory.
    A_in[r, q, s]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (r, q, s) -> (r * NQ + q) * NP + s      # row-major: [r][q][s]

    # Input 2D matrix C4: original C4[s][p], row‑major with p fastest.
    # Layout chosen so that p is unit-stride, which is ideal when we vectorize across p.
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (s, p) -> s * NP + p                   # row-major: [s][p]

    # Output 3D array A_out: same logical shape and layout as A_in, holding the updated A.
    A_out[r, q, p]: out DATA_TYPE =
        (r, q, p) -> (r * NQ + q) * NP + p     # row-major: [r][q][p]

parameters:
    # Tunable tile sizes (compile-time or runtime constants) for cache/blocking.
    TILE_R: int   # e.g. 4   – tile size in r
    TILE_Q: int   # e.g. 8   – tile size in q
    TILE_P: int   # e.g. 64  – tile size in p (must be multiple of VEC_P)
    TILE_S: int   # e.g. 32  – tile size in s (reduction blocking)
    VEC_P:  int   # e.g. 8 or 16 – SIMD width along p, chosen for target CPU

computation:
    # Mathematical definition (matches original PolyBench doitgen):
    # For each (r, q, p):
    #   A_out[r][q][p] = sum_{s=0..NP-1} A_in[r][q][s] * C4[s][p];
    #
    # This is: for each (r,q), a dense matrix–vector product of C4 (NP×NP)
    # with the NP‑vector A_in[r,q,*].
    for r, q, p:
        A_out[r, q, p] = sum(s in [0, NP), A_in[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

optimization:
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Improve arithmetic/data reuse by reordering p and s loops.
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # The high-level semantics are a sum over s, but we are free to
    # change the execution order of (p, s) as addition is associative.
    #
    # Naive loop order implied by the formula:
    #   for r, q, p:
    #       acc = 0
    #       for s: acc += A_in[r,q,s] * C4[s,p]
    #       A_out[r,q,p] = acc
    #
    # We interchange p and s in the accumulation so that for each (r,q)
    # we walk over s *once* and re-use A_in[r,q,s] across all p, while
    # reading a full row C4[s, *] with unit‑stride accesses:
    #
    #   # initialization of all A_out[r,q,*] to 0 kept separate
    #   for r, q:
    #       for p: A_out[r,q,p] = 0
    #       for s:
    #           a = A_in[r,q,s]
    #           for p:
    #               A_out[r,q,p] += a * C4[s,p]
    #
    # This is expressible as a legal loop interchange on p and s.
    interchange(p, s)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Block (tile) r, q, p, and s for cache locality.
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # We tile the three spatial dims r, q, p and the reduction dim s
    # so that work for a small block fits in cache. Blocking s and p
    # together improves locality for C4 and allows re‑use of A_in[r,q,s]
    # across several p values.
    #
    # r -> (R, r)   outer tile index R, inner r within tile
    # q -> (Q, q)   outer tile index Q, inner q within tile
    # p -> (P, p)   outer tile index P, inner p within tile
    # s -> (S, s)   outer tile index S, inner s within tile
    block(r, R, TILE_R)
    block(q, Q, TILE_Q)
    block(p, P, TILE_P)
    block(s, S, TILE_S)

    # After blocking + interchange(p,s), an (informal) loop skeleton is:
    #   for R in [0, NR/TILE_R):
    #     for Q in [0, NQ/TILE_Q):
    #       for r in tile R:
    #         for q in tile Q:
    #           for P in [0, NP/TILE_P):
    #             # zero tile of A_out
    #             for p in tile P: A_out[r,q,p] = 0
    #           for S in [0, NP/TILE_S):
    #             for s in tile S:
    #               a = A_in[r,q,s]
    #               for P in [0, NP/TILE_P):
    #                 for p in tile P:
    #                   A_out[r,q,p] += a * C4[s,p]

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Choose outer parallel dimension(s).
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # (r, q) tiles are fully independent, so we parallelize across the
    # fused outer tiles by parallelizing R, and optionally Q if NR is
    # small compared to available cores.
    #
    # We avoid nested parallel loops here; implementors may fuse (R,Q)
    # into a single parallel dimension if desired.
    parallelize(R)
    # optional: parallelize(Q)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Vectorize along p (contiguous dimension).
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Data layout makes p unit-stride for both C4[s,p] and A_out[r,q,p],
    # so vectorizing p maximizes SIMD efficiency. We do this at the
    # inner p within a tile.
    vectorize(p, VEC_P)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Unroll small inner loops for ILP.
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Unroll a few iterations of the reduction within each S-tile to
    # expose more instruction-level parallelism to the compiler. TILE_S
    # is chosen so that unrolling by a small factor does not bloat code.
    unroll(s, 4)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Optional: hoist tile loops outward for better reuse.
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # We ensure tile loops R and Q are the outermost to maximize reuse
    # of the A_in[r,q,*] and C4 rows within a tile.
    hoist(R)
    hoist(Q)

    # After all optimizations, the effective execution order (per tile)
    # is:
    #
    #   for R, Q in parallel:
    #     for r in tile R:
    #       for q in tile Q:
    #         # initialize A_out[r,q,*] over p, in tiles P, vectorized
    #         for P:
    #           for p (vectorized):
    #             A_out[r,q,p] = 0
    #         # accumulate over s in tiles S, reusing A_in[r,q,s] and
    #         # reading rows of C4 with unit-stride accesses
    #         for S:
    #           for s (unrolled):
    #             a = A_in[r,q,s]
    #             for P:
    #               for p (vectorized):
    #                 A_out[r,q,p] += a * C4[s,p]
    #
    # This preserves the original mathematical result while:
    #   - Reducing redundant loads of A_in[r,q,s] by reusing each value
    #     across the full p-tile.
    #   - Making C4 accesses unit-stride in p.
    #   - Exploiting data parallelism via SIMD on p.
    #   - Exploiting task parallelism across (r,q) tiles.
    #   - Keeping the working set (A tile + A_out tile + C4 rows) cache‑resident.
```
